project_description:
Mollet helps robotics developers test a recorded behavior against a requirement before another training or recovery attempt. Reward curves show change, but not when a posture or motion requirement held. Video provides context, yet watching it repeatedly does not apply the same numeric rule each time. Mollet turns the developer's natural-language intent into an editable behavior condition, aligns it with the robot's location in the video, and evaluates it against the original synchronized telemetry. The workbench reports PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN and shows the matching interval beside the evidence.

The interface supports condition authoring, review, editing, rerunning, approval, and JSON export. Reloading an edited export preserves its values but clears the previous approval, so a changed condition cannot inherit an old review. The evaluator supports time triggers and detects region entry when a SAM box center crosses a boundary. Tracking breaks, observation gaps, or a video too short for the required window return UNKNOWN. The authenticated H1 API example uses only a time trigger. Six recorded Isaac Lab stair-simulation clips are available across H1 biped and Go2 quadruped cases: four have synchronized time series and two are summary-only. Mollet exposes that evidence level instead of treating every clip as equally testable.

In the authenticated H1 example, the authored condition required up-axis alignment of at least 0.8 to start within eight seconds and hold for 0.5 seconds. The original telemetry returned PASS from 0.0 to 0.5 seconds. A reviewer changed the hold to eight seconds and received PASS from 0.0 to 8.0 seconds. A manually authored full-duration 12.48-second Go2 condition returned FAIL. Each result retains condition, observation, video, state, request, and response provenance through hashes, so the evaluation can be replayed without changing the source values.

Mollet builds on our pre-existing RL diagnosis foundation and recorded stair assets. The hackathon contribution is the Meta-powered condition-authoring workflow, frame location binding, deterministic evaluation, review reset, evidence export and reload, saved-response replay, and an extension for video-grounded hypotheses and reflection. The extension registers an original MP4 with synchronized state, derives one to four hypotheses that cite frames present in that source, checks up to three previously untested conditions on the same stored observation, and prepares reflection. A separately confirmed triage probe can support a registered correction proposal after case and correction checks; the proposal stays pending human approval with a GPU budget of zero. These paths passed synthetic-response CPU and browser tests, but no new video-model call, real reflection, reward change, retraining, GPU job, or measured improvement is claimed. Source and evidence are public at https://github.com/mmporong/mollet-meta.
meta_products:
Mollet uses Muse Spark 1.3 and SAM 3.1 through the Meta Responses API, with each model assigned a different, reviewable role. We completed one authenticated Spark call using a natural-language behavior request plus state JSON. Spark returned a constrained contract for the H1 stair recording: up_axis_z greater than or equal to 0.8, an eight-second start deadline, and a 0.5-second hold. This verified Spark call did not analyze raw video. We completed one authenticated SAM 3.1 call on the original H1 simulation video. SAM returned robot boxes for 624 of 625 samples. That figure is response coverage, not tracking accuracy.

Mollet joins the Spark contract and SAM locations to the original synchronized state values rather than asking a model to declare success. The local evaluator applies trigger, deadline, threshold, and hold rules and returns PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN with a time interval. The UI renders video, available boxes, state evidence, and result together. Edits clear prior approval; JSON reload preserves values but requires another review. Request and response hashes, provider identifiers when available, and SHA-bound video, telemetry, and serialized verdict make replay auditable. The replay path distinguishes locally verified raw provider files from a checked-in evidence index and is not presented as a new authenticated call.

We also implemented a Meta video-and-state extension. It builds a request with the registered original MP4 and synchronized state, then validates one to four returned hypotheses against frames in that source. Mollet selects up to three previously untested conditions, evaluates each on the same stored observation, and prepares a Spark reflection request with the verdict, reason, interval, trigger, hashes, and uncertainty. These checks are not new experiments or causal confirmation, and reflection cannot create a confirmed probe. Only a probe independently confirmed by the existing triage loop can enter the correction bridge, where its case and registered correction must match before the ledger records a proposal as pending human approval. The pending proposal has a GPU budget of zero and carries no training approval. Recovery comparison uses the existing fixed oracle or triplet evaluator; neither grants execution approval. Time and SAM box-center region-entry triggers are implemented, although the authenticated H1 call used only time.

The extension was exercised with synthetic model responses in CPU and UI tests. New video inference, real Spark reflection, applied reward correction, retraining, GPU work, and measured recovery improvement are zero. Actual provider evidence remains one Spark and one SAM call. The published 180-second demo was verified playable while logged out; it replays those saved responses in Chrome without a new call. The related suite passed 142 CPU tests and 10 Chrome checks.
why_meta:
Mollet needs Meta's models for structured intent and visual grounding while keeping the behavior verdict reproducible. Muse Spark converts an instruction such as maintaining upright alignment on stairs into a small JSON contract with a metric, threshold, trigger, deadline, and hold duration. SAM supplies the robot's visible location across the source video. Original telemetry and fixed local rules then determine PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN. Spark helps define what to test, SAM helps show where the robot is, and the evaluator establishes whether the recorded measurements satisfy the reviewed condition.

This separation is useful between inspecting a run and deciding what to try next. A robotics developer can see the proposed requirement, edit it, compare the result with the clip, and preserve the exact condition and source hashes before another experiment. The same interface handles H1 biped and Go2 quadruped stair evidence while showing whether a case has synchronized time series or only a summary. It can represent a deadline-based condition or detect when a SAM box center enters a video region. When tracking breaks, observations are missing, or a clip is too short, UNKNOWN tells the reviewer what must be recorded or aligned before evaluation.

The verified Meta calls demonstrate this bridge. Spark authored a condition from natural language and state JSON, SAM supplied 624 boxes across 625 H1 samples, and Mollet joined both to unchanged source telemetry. The result could be reviewed, edited from a 0.5-second hold to an eight-second hold, exported, reloaded with approval reset, and replayed from hashes and saved evidence. Meta output remains inspectable; neither model becomes the final judge or gains permission to change a reward or launch training.

The extension keeps those responsibilities separate in a longer loop. A registered original video and synchronized state support frame-cited hypotheses; up to three untested conditions are evaluated on the same stored observation and carried into reflection with uncertainty intact. These are proxy checks, not new experiments or causal confirmation, and reflection cannot confirm a probe. Only an independently confirmed triage probe can support a correction proposal after case and correction checks; it remains pending human approval, with a GPU budget of zero. Existing fixed evaluation defines how recovery evidence is compared and grants no execution approval. This connects language, visible motion, and measured state without collapsing them into one score. The extension is supported by code and synthetic-response tests, not new inference, real reflection, retraining, or measured recovery gains. We claim a verifiable integration and working review workflow, not model superiority, tracking accuracy, generalization, time savings, or performance improvement.
verified_claims: One authenticated Muse Spark 1.3 call completed from a natural-language request plus state JSON, not raw video.
One authenticated SAM 3.1 call completed on the original H1 video.
The Spark condition was up_axis_z >= 0.8 with an eight-second start deadline and a 0.5-second hold; deterministic evaluation returned PASS from 0.0 to 0.5 seconds.
The H1 evidence contains 625 original state samples and SAM boxes for 624 samples; this is response coverage, not tracking accuracy.
A user-edited eight-second hold returned PASS from 0.0 to 8.0 seconds, and JSON export round-trip preserved values while clearing prior approval.
A manually authored full-duration 12.48-second Go2 condition returned FAIL and was not a new model result.
Six H1 biped and Go2 quadruped stair clips are represented: four with synchronized time series and two with summary-only evidence.
Time-trigger and bounding-box region-entry evaluators are implemented; the authenticated H1 API example used only the time trigger.

The extension can generate one to four frame-cited hypotheses from a registered original MP4 plus synchronized state, select up to three untested conditions, and evaluate each against the same stored observation before preparing reflection; these are not new experiments or causal confirmation.

Reflection cannot confirm a probe; only a probe independently confirmed by the existing triage loop can produce a pending-human-approval correction after case and registered-correction matching, with GPU and training execution still zero.
The related local verification passed 142 CPU tests and 10 Chrome checks.
The 180-second demo uses verified saved historical responses from the two authenticated calls and current Chrome footage; replay made no new model call.
The six H1 and Go2 recordings are from Isaac Lab simulation.
limitations: The verified Spark call used natural language plus state JSON and did not analyze raw video.
The model outputs help author conditions and ground video; they are not the final verdict, human approval, execution authority, or confirmed reward correction.
The extension's new video inference, real reflection, applied reward correction, retraining, GPU use, and measured recovery improvement are all zero in the submitted evidence.
The 624/625 SAM count measures response coverage, not tracking accuracy.
Cross-task generalization, time savings, buyer impact, and performance improvement were not measured.

The RL diagnosis foundation and stair recordings predate the hackathon; the new contribution is the Meta condition-authoring, location-binding, deterministic evaluation, review, export, replay, and staged extension workflow.
